messages.author: 5023feaabf0d4aa7
messages.subject: scale-x issue
parts:
Dear all, seemingly a very simple issue, but I'm experiencing
difficulties in setting the x-axis values directly.
Here are some sample data to illustrate.

#Set the year span from 1999 to 2009
>year=1999:2009
# assign the y-values
>prop=c(.021,.027,.013,.014,.030,.060,.060,.103,.142,.118,.152)

# now plot
>qplot(year,prop)

The x-axis is labelled every 2nd year starting at 2000. If I want to
ensure that every year is labelled I try the following:

> qplot(year,prop, ylab="Proportion",
scale_x_continuous
(breaks=c(1999,2000,2001,2002,2003,2004,2005,2006,2007,2008,2009)))

Again, the plot shows the x-axis unchanged - every 2nd year beginning
with "2000".
I'd appreciate a pointer to how I can ensure that all years are
labelled.

Many thanks,
Alan Kelly
Trinity College Dublin

messages.author: 5196f936ff792c35
messages.subject: Re: scale-x issue
parts:
You were oh so very close. Just put the scale outside the qplot() call. 

qplot(year,prop, ylab="Proportion")+  scale_x_continuous(breaks=c(1999,2000,2001,2002,2003,2004,2005,2006,2007,2008,2009))

brandon

On Mon, Sep 6, 2010 at 10:18, Alan Kelly <ake...@tcd.ie> wrote:
qplot(year,prop, ylab="Proportion",  scale_x_continuous(breaks=c(1999,2000,2001,2002,2003,2004,2005,2006,2007,2008,2009)))

messages.author: 5023feaabf0d4aa7
messages.subject: Re: scale-x issue
parts:
Brandon - I appreciate why you would advise me to "move on" to the more advanced plotting capabilities of ggplot(), but I'm not sure I really agree.  As a biostatistician I am usually juggling many projects and so I need a robust and reasonably sophisticated plotting package - one that offers far more than plot() in the base package, but not necessarily one that offers the full range of tools such as ggplot().  I can only assume that Hadley appreciated this point in that he obviously provided a facility to produce quick (but elegant) plots.  Having said that, it did take me some time to try out various ways to get the x-axis to show each year explicitly and I eventually identified "scale" as the relevant command - but I still needed expert input from yourself to see what I had missed.

I notice that many of the questions to the list seem to require an in-depth understanding of ggplot() to produce the required plot.  Perhaps you would disagree, but I would suggest that for many users of this excellent package, who have neither the need not the leisure to become experts, qplot() - with perhaps some more detailed explanations of its scope  and its options - can serve nearly all our routine needs.

James' suggestion on a function to "translate" qplot() code into ggplot() would be helpful, although I note that Appendix A of Hadley's book offers this in a limited fashion.
Bets wishes,
Alan

messages.author: 5196f936ff792c35
messages.subject: Re: scale-x issue
parts:
I started making graphs with ggplot2 only about 3-4 months ago myself. Mainly screwing around with it and breaking just about everything along the way. Then I bought and read through Hadley's book (filled in some holes). 

I'm no expert, but I have noticed that if you want to fine tune a graph much more than changing an axis title then you really should break it out into the individual components so you can clearly see what is doing what. It also makes it easier to troubleshoot when you give it a new dataset and it gives you an error. You can give it a line at a time and figure out what's erroneous. You can also make new graphs from the parts of others (saves me lots of time). 

Also, as you have seen with just this example, qplot() can use the line by line calls just as easily so it's really not a far cry to go from:
qplot(year,prop, ylab="Proportion")+  scale_x_continuous(breaks=c(1999,2000,2001,2002,2003,2004,2005,2006,2007,2008,2009))

to

#seems to need a dataframe
propyear<-as.data.frame(cbind(year,prop))

ggplot(propyear, aes(x=year, y=prop))+
geom_point()+ 
scale_y_continuous('Proportion')+
scale_x_continuous(breaks=c(1999,2000,2001,2002,2003,2004,2005,2006,2007,2008,2009))

 
That's just my (relatively short) experience with ggplot2 and R.

:/

Brandon
